name: Le Fort I osteotomy
lead: A Le Fort I osteotomy is an orthognathic (jaw) operation in which the upper jaw, or maxilla, is cut horizontally above the roots of the upper teeth, freed, moved to a new position, and fixed in place, commonly with titanium plates and screws [1]. It is used to correct bite problems and skeletal jaw discrepancies such as vertical maxillary excess, to treat cleft-related maxillary deficiency, and as part of maxillomandibular advancement for obstructive sleep apnoea [1][3]. It is also used for facial aesthetic goals, because moving the maxilla changes midface projection and proportion [1].

The surgical literature includes a prospective evaluation of complications in 1000 patients [4], reports of condylar resorption and aseptic necrosis after maxillary osteotomies [5][6], and analyses of long-term stability by direction of movement [7]. Registered trials compare fixation plates and surgical designs [8][9]. In looksmaxxing forums the operation is discussed alongside other jaw and midface procedures, sometimes with disagreement about aesthetic results [10].
infobox: 2-6 weeks initial; 2-4 more months for bone healing [1]

paras: Jaw osteotomies are used for malocclusion from skeletal problems, airway problems including obstructive sleep apnoea, cleft-related growth deficiency, facial asymmetry and aesthetic concerns; maxillary surgery is used for vertical maxillary excess sometimes called long-face syndrome [1]. A 1989 report described maxillomandibular advancement in 23 patients with obstructive sleep apnoea [3], and a 1999 study of 50 patients is cited by Wikipedia as giving 90-100% success for sleep apnoea [1]. Segmental Le Fort I osteotomy has been compared with surgically assisted rapid maxillary expansion for transverse maxillary hypoplasia in a registered trial [11].

The maxilla is moved up, forward or down, and sometimes expanded or segmented. A 1996 review of stability found that stability varies with direction of movement, type of fixation and surgical technique, with superior repositioning of the maxilla described as the most stable orthognathic procedure [7]. Registered trials compare one-piece with segmental osteotomy in cleft patients [12], and compare prebent, custom and patient-specific plates for fixation [8][9].

Orthognathic surgery in general carries risks of bleeding, swelling, infection (reported up to 7% of cases) and nerve damage that causes numbness, usually temporary but rarely permanent [1]. A prospective evaluation of intra- and perioperative complications covered 1000 patients undergoing Le Fort I osteotomy [4]. A 1990 report described 36 cases of aseptic necrosis after maxillary osteotomies [6]. A study of 259 patients with open bite examined condylar remodelling and resorption after Le Fort I and bimaxillary osteotomies [5]. A registered study is examining subclinical optic nerve changes after Le Fort I [13].
Initial healing is reported to take 2 to 6 weeks, with complete bone healing taking a further 2 to 4 months; patients often follow a liquid diet and may have jaw immobilisation for 1 to 4 weeks [1].

On looksmax.org, jaw surgery before-and-after images are debated for their aesthetic effect. One thread compares a patient's pre-operative and post-operative appearance and a poster states being glad to have avoided the procedure, describing the result as unattractive; another poster says they cannot get a Le Fort III for a flat face [10]. Such posts are individual opinions.

Human studies are mainly retrospective or observational: a 1000-patient prospective complication evaluation [4], a 259-patient condylar study [5], a 36-case necrosis report [6], and a 23-patient sleep apnoea series [3]. Registered trials compare fixation and surgical techniques, mostly small [8][9][11][12].

lore.intro: Le Fort I is discussed on looksmax.org as one of the jaw and midface options in appearance surgery, with posters arguing about outcomes in specific before-and-after cases [10].

claims.claim: Le Fort I can produce an unattractive 'chimp mouth' result in some patients.
claims.believers: A poster on looksmax.org shared a surgeon's before-and-after images and said the post-surgical mouth looked worse, expressing relief at not having had the procedure [10].
claims.experts: Published studies address bite correction, stability and complications rather than subjective aesthetic judgments of individual faces [4][7]; the sources reviewed contain no study of how such results are perceived.

card.summary: Cutting and repositioning the upper jaw to fix bite and midface proportion; major surgery with a large clinical literature.
card.note: Major jaw surgery with bleeding, nerve and necrosis risks.

quick.overview:
Le Fort I osteotomy cuts the upper jaw free through the mouth, moves it up, forward or down, and fixes it with plates. It is used for bite problems, long-face deformity, cleft-related deficiency and sleep apnoea, and also changes midface appearance.

The clinical literature is large but mostly observational, covering complications, stability and fixation methods.
quick.mechanism: A horizontal bone cut above the tooth roots frees the maxilla, which is repositioned and fixed, usually with titanium plates and screws [1].
quick.risks: Reported risks include bleeding, swelling, infection, nerve numbness, condylar resorption and rarely aseptic necrosis of the maxilla [1][5][6]. Recovery involves weeks of restricted diet and months of bone healing [1].
